plain: Python is the language AI is going to write your programs in. You're not going to write it: you tell it in plain English what you want, it gives you back some text, you paste it into a file and tell your computer to read it top to bottom. It's like getting a recipe from someone who cooks far better than you: you don't need to know how to invent it, you need to know how to turn on the stove, have the kitchen set up, and notice when something smells like it's burning. Everything that follows here is exactly that and nothing more: setting up the kitchen, turning on the stove, and learning to smell the smoke.

account.free: Free forever. No account, no email, no card, no pro version. It's maintained by a nonprofit foundation and nobody will ever charge you to use it. What does cost money are the AI services you're going to connect to FROM Python: the connector installs for free, but every request you send it is billed separately. While you're practicing, assuming you're going to repeat the same test twenty times, budget between $3 and $10 a month. That's not an official price, it's just what tends to come out; the actual cost depends on the service you pick and how much text you send it.
steps: Type python.org into your browser. In the middle of the page there's a big yellow button that says 'Download Python 3.14.x'. The final number changes every few months, so don't trust the figure you read here: trust the button. Any version in the 3.12, 3.13, or 3.14 series works fine. It downloads a file of about 27 MB ending in .exe. Don't open it yet.
Check the small box at the bottom BEFORE installing

Open the file you downloaded. A dark blue window appears. Right at the bottom, in tiny letters, there's a checkbox that says 'Add python.exe to PATH'. Check it. That two-millimeter checkbox is the difference between everything working on its own and spending the afternoon fighting an error you don't understand.

It's the first of the two big options; it means 'install now with the standard settings'. Takes one to three minutes. Windows will ask if you want to allow the app to make changes: say yes. When it's done it says 'Setup was successful' and sometimes a link shows up that says 'Disable path length limit'. Click that too: it removes an old Windows limit on how long folder names can be, and saves you a weird error down the road.
Check that Windows can see it

Close any command window you had open before installing. Press the Windows key, type PowerShell, and open it: it's the blue window where you type commands as text. Type python --version and press Enter. It should answer with something like 'Python 3.14.2'. If it says it doesn't recognize the name, don't move on: go back to step 2, you didn't check the box.
Create the project folder and its own separate box

In that same window, type one line, Enter, then the other: mkdir C:\Users\YourName\projects\my-first-project and then cd C:\Users\YourName\projects\my-first-project. You're now inside the folder. Now type python -m venv .venv and wait ten seconds. You've just created a folder called .venv inside the project: it's the box where only THIS project's pieces will live, without touching anything else on the computer.

Type .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 and press Enter. If it goes well, (.venv) appears in parentheses at the start of the line. That's the sign you're inside. If PowerShell says 'running scripts is disabled on this system', type once, and only once, Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, answer Y, and activate again. Watch out: activation doesn't stick. Every time you open a new window you have to repeat it.
Install your first package and record the list

With (.venv) showing, type pip install python-dotenv. You'll see lines running by and at the end 'Successfully installed'. Check what you have with pip list. And now the thing almost nobody does and later regrets: type pip freeze > requirements.txt. You've just created a text file with the exact list of what's installed and its version. That file is what you'll paste to the AI when something breaks.
account.warning: Two warnings, and the second one can actually cost you money. One: if you don't check 'Add python.exe to PATH' in step 2, Windows will tell you it doesn't know Python every time you call it. Fix it by opening the same installer again, choosing 'Modify', and checking the box. Don't delete folders by hand or touch system variables. Two: when the AI gives you a line starting with pip install, that command downloads code written by a stranger and runs it on your computer with your permissions. AI sometimes makes up package names that don't exist, and there are people dedicated to registering exactly those made-up names with code inside that hunts for keys and passwords saved on your disk. Before installing something whose name you've never heard, look it up at pypi.org and check that it has thousands of downloads and a real project behind it. Thirty seconds.

first: Open PowerShell, type python --version, and confirm Windows answers with a number. If not, don't move on: the PATH checkbox is missing.
Create the project folder, enter it with cd, run python -m venv .venv, and activate it with .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 until you see the (.venv) in front.
Install something real: pip install python-dotenv, then pip list to see what went into the box.

Copy the 'Empty project ready for vibecoding' template from this guide, create the file check.py, and run it with python check.py. If the list of checks shows up on screen, your setup works and you can now run anything.
Open your AI, paste in the whole CONTEXT.md file from this guide filled with your details, and ask for a five-line first program. Run it. You're already vibecoding.
shortcuts: Up arrow (in PowerShell)

Brings back the last command you typed, and keep pressing it for the ones before that. You're going to run the same python app.py fifty times an afternoon while the AI fixes the program. Typing it out in full every time is wasted time.
Tab key

Autocompletes file and folder names. Type py, press Tab, and it fills in python-dotenv or the file's full name. It also confirms that file really exists and that you're in the right folder, which is half of all bugs.
Ctrl+C (in the command window)
Stops the running program cold. When something hangs, or you've accidentally launched an infinite loop filling the screen, this stops it. It's your handbrake and you'll use it every day.
Right-click inside the blue window

Pastes whatever you have copied. In the classic PowerShell window, Ctrl+V sometimes does nothing and right-click always works. In the Windows 11 Terminal app both work. Since you're going to paste code from the AI constantly, you'll use this a hundred times a day.
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
Enters the project's box. Until you see (.venv) at the start of the line, everything you install goes somewhere else. First command of every session, no exceptions.
python file-name.py
Runs the program. It's literally everything you need to know to test whatever the AI wrote for you. Exact name, with the .py at the end, and while in the folder where that file lives.
pip install -r requirements.txt

Installs everything on that list at once. You switch computers, or a colleague opens your project, and with one line they get your exact setup in two minutes instead of discovering what was missing through a string of errors.
pip freeze > requirements.txt

Records everything currently installed and its exact version into that file. Do it every time you install something new. It's a snapshot of your project: without it, your program only exists on your laptop.
dir
Lists what's in the folder you're in. When the error says it can't find a file, this command tells you in a second whether the file is there, named differently, or you're in a different folder.
cd folder-name  /  cd ..
Enter a folder and step out of it. Almost every bug in your first month is being in the wrong folder, and these two commands are what fix it.
daily: Open the command window ALREADY in the right folder: go into the folder with File Explorer, right-click in an empty spot, and choose 'Open in Terminal' (on Windows 11) or 'Open PowerShell window here' (on Windows 10, holding Shift). Saves you typing out the path by hand.
Activate the environment before anything else and check you see the (.venv) in front. If it's not there, stop and activate it. Everything you do without it ends up in the wrong place.
Run with python file.py and read THE LAST LINE of whatever comes out. The real error is always at the very bottom; what's above is the path the program took before it broke.

Copy the WHOLE error (from the word Traceback to the last line) and paste it to the AI with one sentence: 'I get this when I run it, fix it and give me the complete file.' Don't summarize it or describe it in your own words: paste it as-is.
Install whatever the AI asks for, but check the package name on pypi.org first if you've never heard of it. Thirty seconds that save you from handing your keys to a stranger.
Keep any key, password, or token in the .env file, never inside the code. When the AI writes the key raw into the program, ask it to move it into .env. It'll do it without complaint.
Before closing, pip freeze > requirements.txt. One second. It's what lets you come back tomorrow, or from another computer, and have everything still work.

templates.name: Empty project ready for vibecoding
templates.what: The minimal setup anything you build with AI needs: the folder, the separate box, the file where keys are kept, the list of what not to share, and a check-up program that tells you everything's fine before you start. Good for your first project and every one after it: it's the same five minutes, always.
templates.how: Open PowerShell. Paste the block of commands line by line, waiting for each to finish. For the text files, open Notepad, paste the content, and save with 'Save As', typing the name in quotes (".env", ".gitignore", "check.py") and choosing 'Type: All Files'. Without the quotes, Windows appends .txt and it won't work. At the end run python check.py: if you see the five check-up lines, you can now ask the AI for whatever you want.
fill: Your Windows user folder name. See it by typing echo $env:USERNAME in PowerShell.
Your project's name, no spaces or accents: shirt-shop, appointment-bot, restaurant-site.
The key given to you by whichever AI service you use. It's shown once and never again: save it in your password manager too.
templates.code:
# ============ 1. In PowerShell, one line at a time ============
mkdir C:\Users\YOUR_USER\projects\my-app
cd C:\Users\YOUR_USER\projects\my-app
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# ============ 2. With (.venv) in front, install the basics ============
pip install python-dotenv requests

# ============ 3. File: .env  (keys go here) ============
API_KEY=paste-your-key-here
# No quotes, no spaces around the =, one key per line.

# ============ 4. File: .gitignore  (what does NOT get shared) ============
.venv/
.env
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# ============ 5. File: check.py ============
import os
import sys
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

print("Python version:", sys.version.split()[0])
print("Running from:", sys.executable)
print(".venv environment active:", ".venv" in sys.executable)
print("Current folder:", os.getcwd())

key = os.getenv("API_KEY")
if not key:
    print("FAILED: can't find API_KEY. Check that the .env file")
    print("is in this same folder and is NOT named .env.txt")
else:
    print("Key loaded. Starts with", key[:6], "and has", len(key), "characters")

# ============ 6. Run ============
python check.py

# ============ 7. Save the project snapshot ============
pip freeze > requirements.txt

templates.name: Start with a double-click (start.bat)
templates.what: A file that activates the environment, runs your program, and leaves the window open so you can read the error if there is one. Good for the day your program already works and you want to use it without remembering four commands, and especially for handing it to someone who has no idea what a terminal is: double-click and it works.
templates.how: Open Notepad, paste the content, and save with 'Save As' inside your project's folder (the same one with the .venv folder in it), with the name in quotes: "start.bat", and under 'Type' choose 'All Files'. Double-click and you're done. If Windows warns it's an unknown file, that's normal: you wrote it yourself.
fill: The exact name of the file you want to run, the one the AI wrote for you.
templates.code:
@echo off
rem Moves to the folder this file is in, no matter where the double-click came from
cd /d "%~dp0"

rem Enter the project's box
call .venv\Scripts\activate.bat

rem Run the program
python app.py

echo.
echo ------------------------------------------------
echo The program has finished. If there's an error above,
echo copy it in full and paste it to the AI.
echo ------------------------------------------------
pause

templates.name: Starter requirements.txt
templates.what: The project's shopping list. With this file, anyone (or you yourself six months from now, or on another computer) sets up your whole project with a single command instead of discovering what was missing one error at a time.
templates.how: Create it with Notepad inside the project folder, saving it as "requirements.txt" with the quotes. To install everything it lists: activate the environment and type pip install -r requirements.txt. Once your project already works, replace this file with the exact snapshot using pip freeze > requirements.txt: that also saves the version number of each item, which is what makes it keep working the same way tomorrow.
fill: Remove the hash only from what your project actually uses. If the AI asks you to install something not on the list, add it as a new line.
templates.code:
# What almost every project needs
python-dotenv
requests

# Remove the # in front only of what you actually use:
# openai
# anthropic
# streamlit
# flask
# pandas
# beautifulsoup4

# Install everything here:      pip install -r requirements.txt
# Save the exact snapshot:      pip freeze > requirements.txt

templates.name: CONTEXT.md: what you paste to the AI at the start of every session
templates.what: A piece of text you paste to the AI at the start of every new conversation so it knows who you are, what computer you have, and how to talk to you. Without this, it'll give you Mac instructions when you're on Windows, hand you loose fragments of code you don't know where to put, and assume you know ten things you don't. With this, it stops doing that.
templates.how: Create the file with Notepad inside the project folder, with the name in quotes: "CONTEXT.md". Fill in the brackets. Every time you open a new conversation with the AI, open it, copy it all, and paste it as your first message. Update the two 'what I already have' sections by pasting the output of the dir and pip list commands every few days.
fill: One sentence in plain English: 'a website where my customers book appointments'.
Your Windows username and the project folder's name.
Paste the output of typing dir in the project folder.
Paste the output of typing pip list with the environment active.
templates.code:
# PROJECT CONTEXT

## WHAT I'M BUILDING
[One sentence: "a website where my customers book appointments"]

## MY SETUP
- Windows 11, I use PowerShell.
- Python installed from python.org with "Add python.exe to PATH" checked.
- Project folder: C:\Users\[YOUR_USER]\projects\[NAME]
- Virtual environment .venv inside that folder.
  I activate it with: .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
- I keep keys in a .env file and read them with python-dotenv.
- Programming level: zero. I can't read code and I'm not going to learn.

## FILES I ALREADY HAVE
[Paste here the output of typing: dir]

## WHAT I'VE ALREADY INSTALLED
[Paste here the output of typing: pip list]

## HOW I WANT YOU TO TALK TO ME
1. Always tell me which folder I need to be in before running anything.
2. Give me COMPLETE files, from the first line to the last.
   Never loose fragments or "...same as before...".
3. Tell me the exact file name and where to save it.
4. One step at a time. Wait for me to say it worked.
5. If something deletes files, sends emails, publishes anything, or
   costs money, warn me BEFORE and explain what's going to happen.
6. If you ask me to install a package, tell me what it's for in one sentence.

errors: python : The term 'python' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet, function, script file, or operable program.

Python isn't missing: Windows doesn't know which folder to look in. It's the 'Add python.exe to PATH' checkbox left unchecked. Fix: open the same installer you downloaded again, choose 'Modify', click Next, and check that box. Close every PowerShell window and open a new one; old ones keep the old list. The same error with the word pip instead of python has exactly the same cause and the same fix.
Cannot load the file C:\Users\...\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 because running scripts is disabled on this system.

Windows ships by default without allowing command scripts to run, for security. Type once, and only once: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned. It'll ask if you're sure: answer Y and Enter. It only affects your user, not the whole computer. Then type .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 again and you'll see the (.venv) appear.

The program is asking for a piece that isn't installed in the box you're in. It's almost always one of two things: either you didn't activate the (.venv) before installing and the package went into the general Python, or you simply haven't installed it yet. Fix: check that you see (.venv) at the start of the line and type pip install followed by the name shown in quotes in the error. Watch out for one detail: the name you install isn't always the one shown in the error (here the package is called python-dotenv, but the error says dotenv). If pip says it doesn't exist, ask the AI: 'to import dotenv, what package do I need to install with pip?'
python: can't open file 'C:\Users\you\app.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory

You're in the wrong folder, or the file is named differently than you think. Type dir to see what's really there. Two common traps: Notepad saves it as app.py.txt if you don't put the name in quotes when saving, and capitalization and accented characters count. Use Tab to autocomplete the name: if Tab doesn't complete it, that file isn't there.

In Python, the spaces at the start of each line mean something: they mark what belongs inside what, like paragraph breaks in a letter. Copying and pasting from the chat can slip in extra or missing spaces. Don't try to fix it yourself by counting spaces. Go back to the chat, ask 'give me the complete file again, from the first line to the last', copy it using the code block's own copy button (not by selecting with the mouse), and paste the whole file over the old one.

You've pasted something into the file that isn't code: the sentence the AI wrote before the code block, the three backticks ``` that wrap code in the chat, or two versions of the same program stacked on top of each other. Open the file and delete everything that isn't code. If in doubt, delete the whole file, ask for 'the complete file and only the file, no explanations', and paste that.
ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement openaii (from versions: none)

That package doesn't exist under that name. Either it's a typo, or the AI made it up, which happens more than you'd think. Do NOT try similar names until one sticks: that's exactly where fake packages with malicious code inside are lurking. Look up the name at pypi.org, check that it has downloads and a real project behind it, and use the name given on the tool's official page.
UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\u2705' in position 0

The program is trying to print an emoji or odd character that the Windows command window doesn't know how to draw. It's not your fault and nothing important is broken. Quick fix: ask the AI to 'remove the emojis from the messages the program prints'. If you need to keep them, ask it to open files with encoding="utf-8".

prompts.name: Have the AI set up the whole project from scratch, assuming nothing
prompts.prompt: Act as a programming teacher working with someone starting from absolute zero. I've never coded, I'm not going to learn to write code, and I can't read it. I work on Windows 11 with PowerShell. I have Python installed from python.org with the 'Add python.exe to PATH' box checked, and I know how to create and activate a virtual environment with python -m venv .venv and .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1. I don't know anything else. I want to build this: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE WHAT YOU WANT: for example, a website where my customers book appointments and I get notified]. Set it up for me from scratch with these rules, and follow every one of them: first, tell me what we're going to build in four sentences and what files the project will have, before writing a single line. Second, give me ONE step at a time and wait for me to say it worked before giving me the next; don't dump twenty steps on me at once. Third, in every step tell me which folder I need to be in, which file I need to create, its exact name, and where it goes. Fourth, always give me the COMPLETE files, from the first line to the last, never fragments or 'here's what goes before'. Fifth, if something needs installing with pip, tell me in one sentence what that package is for and confirm the name exists exactly as written on pypi.org. Sixth, no keys or passwords inside the code: they go in a .env file we'll read with python-dotenv. Seventh, if any step deletes files, sends messages, publishes something, or costs money, warn me BEFORE, in bold, and tell me how much it costs. Start with step one.

prompts.name: Paste an error and have it fixed without breaking what already worked
prompts.prompt: I have an error running my program and I don't know how to read code, so I need you to fix it and give me the whole file ready to paste. My setup: Windows 11, PowerShell, virtual environment .venv active (I see the (.venv) at the start of the line). I'm in the folder [YOUR FOLDER PATH, e.g. C:\Users\Ana\projects\my-app]. The command I ran was [THE EXACT COMMAND, e.g. python app.py]. Here's what shows on screen, copied in full from the first line to the last, nothing removed: [PASTE THE COMPLETE ERROR HERE]. And here's the file exactly as I have it right now, copied in full: [PASTE YOUR FILE HERE]. Do this in this order: first, explain in two sentences and no technical words what happened and why, as you'd explain it to someone who's never seen the inside of a computer. Second, tell me whether the bug is in the code, in something missing that needs installing, in the folder I'm in, or in the configuration; I want to know what type it is. Third, give me the COMPLETE corrected file, from the first line to the last, no cuts, so I can delete mine and paste yours as-is. Fourth, tell me exactly what command to run to test it and what should show on screen if it worked. Fifth, if the fix changes something that used to work, tell me clearly. If you're missing any information to be sure, ask before touching anything: I'd rather answer one question than try three blind fixes.

prompts.name: Have it explain what the code does BEFORE you run it
prompts.prompt: I'm going to paste a program you wrote for me (or that I found somewhere) and I want to understand what it does before running it on my computer. I can't read code, so don't translate it line by line with jargon: tell me the way you'd explain to a friend what a machine does. Here's the code: [PASTE THE CODE HERE]. Answer me with these five sections, in this order and with these headings. One, WHAT IT DOES: three or four sentences in plain English covering the program's path from start to finish. Two, WHAT IT TOUCHES ON MY COMPUTER: tell me whether it creates files, modifies them, DELETES anything, which folders it touches, and whether it moves or copies things. If it deletes or overwrites anything, put that first and in caps. Three, WHAT IT SENDS OUT: tell me whether it connects to the internet, to which exact service, what information leaves my computer, and whether that information includes personal data, emails, or keys. Four, WHAT IT MIGHT COST ME: if it calls a paid service, tell me which one, roughly how much each run costs in dollars, and whether there's a risk of runaway spending from a loop or a bug. Five, WHAT CAN GO WRONG: the two or three most likely failures the first time and what message I'll see. At the end, give me your recommendation in one line: run it as-is, run it with a change, or better not to run it. If anything in the code doesn't add up or seems to do more than it says, tell me plainly.

prompts.name: Pull the keys out of the code and secure the project before showing it to anyone
prompts.prompt: I want to make my project secure before showing it to someone, uploading it to the internet, or pasting the code in a chat to ask for help. I don't know how to code and I need hands-on instructions, not theory. My setup: Windows 11, PowerShell, Python with a .venv virtual environment, project folder at [YOUR FOLDER PATH]. Here are my files: [PASTE THE CONTENT OF YOUR FILES, OR AT LEAST THE MAIN ONE]. Do the following. One, review the code and tell me if there's any key, password, token, email address, phone number, or personal data written directly inside. Show me the exact line where each one is. Two, give me the corrected version of each file, COMPLETE, where all that data is read from a .env file using python-dotenv, with clear names for each value. Three, give me the exact content my .env file needs to have, with the values left blank for me to fill in. Four, give me the exact content of a .gitignore file that prevents accidentally sharing the .env, the .venv folder, and any file with data. Five, tell me which files in my project I can show without worry and which ones I should NEVER paste into a chat or upload anywhere. Six, if I've ever pasted a key into a chat, an email, or a website, tell me exactly what I need to do to revoke it and get a new one, and warn me if that breaks anything currently working. Be specific with file names and paths.

prompts.name: Package the project so it also works outside your computer
prompts.prompt: My program already works on my computer and I want to be able to set it up again in six months, hand it to someone else, or take it to another laptop without it breaking. I don't know how to code, give me hands-on steps. My setup: Windows 11, PowerShell, Python with a .venv virtual environment inside the project folder, which is at [YOUR FOLDER PATH]. Here's what I have installed, copied from typing pip list: [PASTE THE OUTPUT OF pip list HERE]. And here are my files, copied from typing dir: [PASTE THE OUTPUT OF dir HERE]. I want you to do five things. One, tell me which files on that list are essential for the project to work and which are junk I can delete without worry. Two, give me the exact command to generate the requirements.txt file and explain in two sentences why it's the piece that makes this work on another computer. Three, write me a complete LEEME.txt (README) file, in English and with no jargon, with step-by-step instructions someone who's never coded would need to follow to set up this project from scratch on a clean Windows machine: installing Python, creating the environment, activating it, installing the list, and running it. Four, tell me what should NOT go in the folder I hand that person, especially the keys file, and what they need to do to set up their own. Five, warn me about what most commonly breaks when moving a project from one computer to another and how I avoid it starting today. Give me the complete files, ready to save.

words: pip

The delivery person. You type pip install and a name, and in twenty seconds you have on your computer a piece of program that took someone two years to write. It comes bundled with Python; no separate install needed. It's the command you'll type the most after python.
Virtual environment (.venv)

A closed box inside your project's folder where everything that project needs gets stored, without mixing with everything else. A separate toolbox per job, instead of one shared pile on the table. If you throw one box away, the rest of the computer doesn't even notice.
Package or library

A piece of program someone wrote, tested, and gave away so you don't have to write it yourself. Connecting to an AI service is three lines of your own and ten thousand lines that already came built into the package.
Script (.py file)

An ordinary text file, ending in .py, with instructions inside, one per line. It's run by typing python and its name. It starts at the top, works its way down, and stops at the end. You can open it with Notepad: inside, it's just text.
Terminal, PowerShell, command line

Three names for the same thing: the blue window where you type commands as text instead of clicking buttons. You type a line, press Enter, the computer answers below. Nothing you type there happens until you press Enter, so you can read it twice first.
Traceback

The wall of lines that shows up when something fails. It's read BACKWARDS: the last line is the real error, and what's above is the path the program took before it broke. You don't need to understand it: you need to copy it in full and paste it to the AI.
requirements.txt

An ordinary text file with your project's shopping list: what you've installed and its exact version. Hand it to someone else, or to yourself a year from now, and in a minute they have your exact setup with no guesswork.
.env

A text file where keys and passwords are kept, separate from the code. It exists so you can show your program to anyone without handing over your keys. It's the file that NEVER gets shared, pasted into a chat, or uploaded anywhere.
PATH

The list of folders Windows checks when you type a program's name. If Python's folder isn't on that list, Windows will swear Python doesn't exist even though you're looking right at it installed on the disk.
Indentation

The blank spaces at the start of a line of code. In Python they're not decoration: they mark what belongs inside what. That's why a bad copy-paste can break the program even though every word is there.
matters: Always know two things before pressing Enter: which folder you're in and whether you see the (.venv) at the start of the line. Most bugs in your first month aren't code bugs, they're being in the wrong place or installing into the wrong box. It hurts because you start hunting for a flaw in a program that was perfectly fine, and you can lose a whole afternoon on something a quick dir would have shown at a glance.

Paste the AI the COMPLETE error, exactly as it shows, not your own summary. When you write 'I get a module error' instead of pasting the fifteen lines, you strip out exactly the detail it needed: the exact name, the line number, the file. It starts guessing, you try three fixes that weren't it, and the project ends up worse than when you started because every attempt touched something.

Keys should live in .env, not inside the code. The AI will write them raw into the program if you don't tell it otherwise, because that makes the example shorter. The day you paste that file into a chat to ask for help, or upload it somewhere, that key belongs to anyone. Revoking it and getting a new one is half an hour, and if someone's already used it, you're the one who pays the bill.

Read what a program does before running it, even if you don't understand the code. You don't have to read the code: you have to ask the AI itself whether that program deletes files, sends anything out of your computer, or costs money, and not run it until you have the answer. A program that deletes files deletes them for real, they don't go to the recycle bin, and there's no undo.
ignore: Learning Python's grammar: classes, objects, decorators, list comprehensions. You're not going to write code, you're going to request it. Knowing that a .py file runs top to bottom and that indentation means 'this goes inside that' is more than enough for your first year.

The debate over which package manager to use: conda, poetry, pipenv, uv. Each has its defenders and good reasons, all of them valid. venv and pip come bundled with Python, there's nothing to install, and they cover ninety-five percent of what you'll do. You'll pick a side the day something specific starts bothering you.

The yellow warnings pip throws out: 'notice: A new release of pip is available', 'DeprecationWarning', 'WARNING: You are using pip version...'. They're reminders, not errors. If the program does what it was supposed to, keep going. Only worry when the word Error shows up or the program stops.

questions.prompt: You installed Python yesterday afternoon and the installer said everything went fine. Today you open PowerShell, type python --version, and Windows answers: "python is not recognized as an internal or external command." You check, and Python's folder is right there, at C:\Users\YourName\AppData\Local\Programs\Python. What do you do?

options.text: I reopen the same installer I downloaded, choose 'Modify', and this time check 'Add python.exe to PATH'
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is in what the error actually says: it doesn't say 'Python isn't installed', it says 'I don't recognize that word'. Windows only looks for programs in a specific list of folders, and Python's folder never made it onto that list. The installer adds it for you in thirty seconds; doing it by hand in the system variables is where people end up touching what they shouldn't.

options.text: I delete everything and download Python again from scratch, because the installation must be corrupted
options.why: It's what the message suggests if you read it fast, which is why half the internet does it. But you just saw the folder with the files inside yourself: the program is intact. Reinstalling might accidentally fix it if you check the box this time, and if you skip it again you'll have the exact same error and half an hour less.

options.text: I type py --version instead of python --version, see that it works, and move on with that
options.why: It really does work, which is why it's deceptive: Windows separately installs a small launcher called py that does get registered. The problem shows up two minutes later, when you type pip install openai on its own, because pip lives in that same invisible folder and there's no shortcut there. And every instruction you'll read over the next year starts with python or pip.

questions.explain: That error never means Python is missing: it means Windows doesn't know which folder to look in.

questions.prompt: You've been working on a project using the openai library for two weeks and it works. You start a second project following a year-old tutorial that asks for an older version of that same library. You install it, the tutorial works, and the next day you go back to the first project: now it fails on a line you never touched.

options.text: I create a .venv folder inside each project, activate it before installing, and in each one put the version that project asks for
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is that this isn't a patch, it's the normal way to work: the two projects are going to coexist forever asking for different things. With one environment per folder, each has its own version and neither knows the other exists. The first project works again as soon as you install inside its own box whatever its requirements.txt says.

options.text: I uninstall and reinstall whichever version I need every time I switch projects
options.why: It's tempting because it works: for one afternoon, with two projects and one library, it's perfectly manageable. It breaks once each project has a dozen packages installed, and each of those drags in others you didn't even know were there. No human memory can keep up with that, and you end up switching projects afraid of what'll break.

options.text: I upgrade both to the latest version with pip install --upgrade and adapt the old tutorial
options.why: Sounds reasonable because newer is usually better and nobody wants to be stuck behind. But the tutorial asked for that older version for a specific reason: some function's name changed between versions and the example code no longer fits. You've just started rewriting a tutorial you don't understand yet to save yourself one seven-word line.

questions.explain: One toolbox per job. Mix every job into the same toolbox and fixing one breaks another.
